top_choice_rationale: P002 (Kiyotaki and Moore, B006) rewards a single mechanism with unambiguous originators. Borrowing limits tied to collateral values make asset prices and credit reinforce each other, so temporary shocks become large, persistent and propagated across sectors. This is the limited-enforcement logic of financial contracting aggregated into general equilibrium. The 1997 paper is the origin, and nearly thirty years of extension, quantification and crisis-era application settle maturity. A citation can be written without a contestable cut. It can state the difference from the 2022 prize by naming collateral, asset prices and credit cycles and not banks or runs. The main weakness is that the amplification is identified indirectly and the contribution is mainly theoretical. P001 (Autor, Hanson, Katz, B027) is a very strong second, with broader and more directly tested evidence, but it carries a real attribution cost: Dorn is excluded, the technology and trade strands may be two achievements joined by Autor, and the task-framework credit extends beyond the named laureates. I rank both well above no award, since each is a mature, important and defensible achievement. I do not treat the breadth of support for P001 as evidence of merit.
recusal_note: No co-authorship or institutional tie to Kiyotaki, Moore, Autor, Hanson or Katz is apparent from my profile. I am an adjunct professor at Chicago Booth, and my principal co-author Steven Kaplan is not credited on any shortlisted ballot. I have long committee overlap with Hassler and Krusell, and I am KVA Vice President and a former committee chair. My research field of finance and contracting may bias me toward B006. These ties are disclosed, not adjudicated.
